title: The 12 Principles
subtitle: The classic rules that bring drawings to life

lessons.title: Squash & Stretch
lessons.summary: Soft things squash and stretch as they move.

steps.title: Squish!
steps.text: When a soft ball hits the ground, it squashes flat. When it moves fast, it stretches long. This makes things feel soft and alive. The trick: the ball never gets bigger or smaller overall. If it gets wider, it gets shorter.

steps.title: Stiff or squishy?
steps.text: Both balls bounce with the same timing. The left one stays perfectly round, so it feels hard, like a marble. The right one squashes and stretches, so it feels soft and bouncy.

steps.title: Three squashy drawings
steps.text: Draw the ball falling (stretched tall), hitting the ground (squashed flat), then bouncing up (round).
steps.hint: Stretched means tall and thin. Squashed means short and wide.

quiz.question: When the ball squashes flat, it should also...
quiz.explain: It keeps the same amount of ball: flatter means wider.

lessons.title: Anticipation
lessons.summary: Get ready before the big move.

steps.title: Get ready...
steps.text: Before a big move, there's a small move the other way. Before you jump, you crouch down. Before you throw, you pull your arm back. This is anticipation: it tells the audience something is about to happen.

steps.title: Big move, big wind-up
steps.text: The bigger the action, the bigger the anticipation. A little hop needs only a little crouch. A huge jump needs a deep crouch.

steps.title: Crouch, then jump
steps.text: Draw the bean standing, crouching down low, stretching up as it takes off, then up in the air.
steps.hint: The crouch is short and wide, the take-off is tall and thin.

quiz.question: A character is about to punch. What's the anticipation?
quiz.explain: Pulling back first warns the audience that a punch is coming.

lessons.title: Staging
lessons.summary: Show the idea so clearly nobody can miss it.

steps.title: Make it clear
steps.text: Staging means showing your idea so clearly that nobody can miss it. Put the important thing where the eye goes, keep the background simple, and give it room.

steps.title: The silhouette test
steps.text: Imagine your character filled in solid black. Can you still tell what it's doing? On the left the arms are hidden in front of the body. On the right they stick out, so the pose reads instantly.

steps.title: A clear pose
steps.text: Trace a waving pose with the arms well clear of the body.
steps.hint: Head and body first, then the legs, then the arms.

quiz.question: How can you check if a pose is clear?
choices: Fill it in black and see if you can still tell what's happening
quiz.explain: If the silhouette reads, the pose reads.

lessons.title: Straight Ahead & Pose to Pose
lessons.summary: Two ways to plan an animation.

steps.title: Two ways to animate
steps.text: Straight ahead: draw frame 1, then 2, then 3, in order, making it up as you go. It's great for wild things like fire and water. Pose to pose: draw the important key poses first, then fill in the frames between them, called inbetweens. It's great for planned acting.

steps.title: Keys first, then inbetweens
steps.text: Here's pose to pose: first the two keys (the ends of the swing), then a breakdown in the middle, then the inbetweens. Notice the inbetweens bunch up near the ends, where the swing slows down.

steps.title: Swing the pendulum
steps.text: Draw one swing from left to right. Put drawings close together at the ends and further apart in the middle.
steps.hint: The pendulum is slowest at the ends of its swing and fastest at the bottom.

quiz.question: Which way works best for a wild, flickering fire?
quiz.explain: Fire changes shape all the time, so drawing it frame after frame keeps it lively.

lessons.title: Follow Through
lessons.summary: Loose parts keep moving after the body stops.

steps.title: Keep going, then settle
steps.text: When a character stops, not everything stops at once. Hair, ears, a tail or an antenna keep going, then swing back and settle. This is follow through.

steps.title: Overlapping action
steps.text: Different parts move at different times. When you wave, your shoulder moves first, then your elbow, then your hand, each a little later. That delay makes motion feel loose and real.

steps.title: The antenna catches up
steps.text: The critter just stopped. Draw the antenna leaning forward, swinging back, then standing still.
steps.hint: First the antenna overshoots forward, then it swings back a little, then it settles.

quiz.question: A dog runs and stops suddenly. What do its floppy ears do?
choices: Keep moving forward, then swing back and settle
Stop at exactly the same time
quiz.explain: Loose parts carry on moving, then settle: that's follow through.

lessons.title: Slow In & Slow Out
lessons.summary: Speed up gently, slow down gently.

steps.title: Gentle starts and stops
steps.text: Things rarely start or stop instantly. A car starts slowly, speeds up, then slows down before it stops. To show this, put drawings close together near the start and end (slow) and further apart in the middle (fast). The ticks underneath show where each drawing goes.

steps.title: Spacing charts
steps.text: Animators plan spacing with a little chart. Each tick is one frame. Ticks close together mean slow; ticks far apart mean fast. Watch the three balls: same start, same end, different spacing.

steps.title: Slow to a stop
steps.text: The ball rolls in fast and slows down to a stop. Make each gap smaller than the one before.
steps.hint: Big gap, smaller gap, smaller still, tiny gap.

quiz.question: The gaps between drawings get smaller and smaller. The thing is...
quiz.explain: Smaller gaps mean it moves less each frame, so it's slowing down.

steps.title: Curves, not lines
steps.text: Living things move along curves, not straight lines. A swinging arm, a turning head, a thrown ball: they all follow arcs. Motion in straight lines looks stiff and robotic. The orange line is the path of the hand.

steps.title: A thrown ball
steps.text: Gravity bends a thrown ball's path into a smooth arc: up, over and down.

steps.title: Trace the arc
steps.text: Trace the path of a thrown ball in one smooth move.
steps.hint: Keep it smooth over the top. No flat spots or corners.

steps.title: Along the arc
steps.text: Draw the ball at each point along the arc.
steps.hint: Follow the orange arc with each ball.

quiz.question: Why animate along arcs?
quiz.explain: Joints swing and gravity pulls, so real motion curves.

lessons.title: Secondary Action
lessons.summary: Small extra moves that add personality.

steps.title: A little extra
steps.text: A secondary action is a small extra movement that supports the main one. A character walks (the main action) while their bag swings, or they whistle, or they wipe their brow. It adds personality, but it should never steal the show.

steps.title: Bean with a bag
steps.text: Trace the bean and its swinging bag.
steps.hint: Draw the bean first, then the strap, then the bag.

quiz.question: Which is a secondary action for someone walking?
quiz.explain: The legs are the main action. The flapping scarf adds to it.

quiz.question: A secondary action should...
choices: Support the main action without stealing attention
Be bigger than the main action
Only happen when nothing else moves
quiz.explain: It's a supporting actor, not the star.

lessons.title: Timing
lessons.summary: More frames is slower, fewer is faster.

steps.title: Frames are time
steps.text: Timing is how many frames an action takes. More frames make it slower. Fewer frames make it faster. Both balls travel the same distance, but the top one does it in 4 frames and the bottom one in 12.

steps.title: Timing shows weight
steps.text: Timing also shows how heavy something is. Heavy things take longer to get going and longer to stop. Light things zip around. At 12 frames per second, 12 frames is one second.

steps.title: Make it quick
steps.text: Zip the ball across the page in just 3 frames, with even gaps.
steps.hint: Big, even jumps make it fast.

quiz.question: At 12 frames per second, how long is 24 frames?
quiz.explain: 24 frames divided by 12 frames each second is 2 seconds.

lessons.title: Exaggeration
lessons.summary: Push it further to make it fun.

steps.title: Push it!
steps.text: Real life can look dull when it's animated. Exaggeration pushes things further: a bigger squash, a higher jump, a wider smile. Push it until it's fun, but keep it believable.

steps.title: Totally shocked
steps.text: Trace this exaggerated surprised face: huge eyes, raised brows, round open mouth.
steps.hint: Big circle first, then the eyes, then the mouth and brows.

quiz.question: What does exaggeration do?
choices: Makes actions clearer and more fun
Makes the drawing look like a photo
quiz.explain: Pushing a pose makes the feeling easier to read.

lessons.title: Solid Drawing
lessons.summary: Draw things with weight and volume.

steps.title: Think in 3D
steps.text: Solid drawing means drawing things as real objects with weight and volume, not flat cut-outs. Think of every shape as a box, ball or tube that you could pick up and turn around.

steps.title: Draw a box
steps.text: Trace the box. See how it shows its top and two sides?
steps.hint: Do the three lines that meet at the front corner first.

quiz.question: Which shows solid drawing?
choices: A box showing its top and two sides
quiz.explain: Showing more than one side gives the box volume.

lessons.title: Appeal
lessons.summary: Characters that are fun to look at.

steps.title: Fun to watch
steps.text: Appeal is what makes a character fun to look at. It doesn't just mean cute: villains need appeal too! A great trick is to mix big, medium and small shapes instead of making everything the same size.

steps.title: Big, medium, small
steps.text: Trace the character: a big body, a small head and medium feet.
steps.hint: Start with the biggest shape, the body.

quiz.question: Which design has more appeal?
choices: Shapes in different sizes: big, medium and small
quiz.explain: Contrast in size makes a design interesting to look at.
